title: What does it mean to use AI critically? Unpacking critical AI literacy through students' evaluation of AI-generated content
summary: Although critical AI literacy has emerged as an important educational goal, the construct remains conceptually broad and insufficiently specified for guiding students' day-to-day interactions with AI. This study examines how students critically evaluated AI-generated content. Drawing on an analysis of students' chatbot interactions and written reflections, we first identified seven stages of AI-supported academic task completion and five functional roles assumed by AI. More importantly, we identified eight evaluative lenses that students used to assess AI-generated responses (accuracy, completeness, task alignment/relevance, personalization, practicality, creativity, ethics, and bias). The findings suggest that critical AI literacy extends beyond verifying the factual accuracy of AI-generated information. Rather, critically engaging with AI involves situated and multidimensional judgment about the epistemic quality, contextual fit, practical feasibility, creative value, and ethical implications of AI-generated content. The framework offers both a conceptual contribution to the emerging literature on critical AI literacy and a practical tool for educators seeking to help learners move from passive acceptance of AI toward deliberate, context-sensitive, and responsible human judgment.

AI.tldr: The study develops a multidimensional framework for critical AI literacy by analyzing how students use and evaluate AI-generated content during academic tasks. It identifies seven stages of AI-supported task completion, five AI functional roles, and eight evaluative lenses: accuracy, completeness, task alignment/relevance, personalization, practicality, creativity, ethics, and bias.
AI.motivation: Critical AI literacy is increasingly important, but existing definitions are broad and provide limited guidance for students' everyday interactions with AI. The study addresses this gap by examining how students actually judge AI-generated responses in academic contexts.
AI.method: The researchers analyzed students' chatbot interactions and written reflections. From these data, they identified seven stages of AI-supported academic task completion, five functional roles played by AI, and eight dimensions students used to evaluate AI-generated content.
AI.result: Students evaluated AI outputs through multidimensional and context-sensitive judgments, not merely factual verification. Their evaluations considered epistemic quality, completeness, relevance to the task, personalization, practical feasibility, creative value, ethical implications, and bias.
AI.conclusion: Critical AI literacy should be understood as the ability to make deliberate, situated, and responsible judgments about AI-generated content. The proposed framework contributes conceptually to critical AI literacy research and offers educators a practical basis for moving students beyond passive acceptance toward informed human oversight.

title: AI-Mediated Self: How HCI Defines and Relates to the Self
summary: How might AI alter how we understand and experience the self? This scoping review analyzes 102 papers to examine how the self is defined in the field of human-computer interaction (HCI), how AI-self relationships are conceptualized, and what risks emerge when AI becomes entangled with selfhood. Our synthesis makes three contributions. First, we define AI-mediated self as a conceptual umbrella that connects dispersed work across education, workplace, health, and creative practices. Second, we consolidate six framings of the self with four domains of ethical risk-agency/autonomy, identity/authorship, relational capacity, and meaning-making-into a conceptual map that provides a reusable vocabulary across contexts. Third, we introduce the Inclusion of AI-Self framework, which situates AI-self relationships along a spectrum of proximity. Together, these contributions position selfhood as a central design space in HCI.

AI.tldr: This scoping review synthesizes 102 HCI papers to explain how AI reshapes conceptions of selfhood and to map the associated ethical risks. It proposes the concept of the AI-mediated self, organizes prior work into six framings of the self and four ethical-risk domains, and introduces the Inclusion of AI-Self framework to classify AI-self relationships by proximity.
AI.motivation: AI is increasingly integrated into education, work, healthcare, and creative activities, but HCI research treats its effects on selfhood in fragmented ways. The review addresses the need for a shared conceptual vocabulary and a systematic account of the ethical risks that arise when AI becomes part of how people understand, express, and construct themselves.
AI.method: The paper conducts a scoping review of 102 HCI papers. It synthesizes how these studies define the self, how they conceptualize relationships between AI and selfhood, and what risks they identify. The synthesis produces a conceptual umbrella, a map connecting six self-related framings with four ethical-risk domains, and a spectrum-based framework for describing the proximity of AI to the self.
AI.result: The review identifies three main contributions: (1) the concept of the AI-mediated self, linking dispersed research across multiple application domains; (2) a reusable conceptual map combining six framings of the self with risks concerning agency and autonomy, identity and authorship, relational capacity, and meaning-making; and (3) the Inclusion of AI-Self framework, which positions AI-self relationships along a continuum of proximity.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues that selfhood should be treated as a central design concern in HCI rather than a peripheral consequence of AI deployment. Its frameworks support more consistent analysis of how AI participates in personal identity, agency, relationships, and meaning-making, while helping designers and researchers anticipate ethical harms.

title: Guided Reflection for Personal Sleep Insight in Everyday Sleep Tracking
summary: Digital sleep technologies make tracking accessible, yet users often struggle to interpret what changes in their sleep mean. Behavioral sleep medicine addresses this through guided discovery, helping patients develop personal interpretations rather than simply receiving explanations. To bring this to everyday tracking, we present DREAM, an LLM-powered voice assistant that monitors conversational sleep diaries, selectively invites users to interpret meaningful changes, and uses their interpretation to tailor subsequent education. We co-designed DREAM with sleep specialists iteratively and evaluated it in a six-week field study (N=14) against a generic-education control. DREAM participants reported greater personal sleep insight, motivation, and willingness to use the system, and described a clearer rationale for trying strategies. Our findings suggest that guided reflection made participants more active interpreters of their own sleep. Furthermore, we argue that expert involvement is not a single transfer of knowledge but an ongoing process of making tacit judgment explicit and testable.

AI.tldr: The paper presents DREAM, an LLM-powered voice assistant that applies guided discovery to help people interpret personal sleep changes and use those interpretations to receive tailored education. In a six-week study with 14 participants, DREAM outperformed generic education on perceived sleep insight, motivation, willingness to use the system, and understanding of why to try sleep strategies.
AI.motivation: Although digital sleep trackers make monitoring easy, users often cannot determine what observed changes mean or how to act on them. Behavioral sleep medicine uses guided discovery—prompting people to develop and test their own interpretations—to support meaningful behavior change. The paper aims to translate this expert-guided process into an everyday conversational sleep-tracking system while preserving the interpretive role of users and sleep specialists.
AI.method: The authors co-designed DREAM iteratively with sleep specialists. DREAM is an LLM-powered voice assistant that monitors conversational sleep diaries, identifies potentially meaningful changes, selectively prompts users to interpret those changes, and uses their interpretations to tailor subsequent sleep education. It was evaluated in a six-week field study with 14 participants, comparing DREAM with a generic-education control condition.
AI.result: Compared with generic education, DREAM participants reported greater personal insight into their sleep, stronger motivation, greater willingness to continue using the system, and a clearer rationale for trying recommended strategies. Qualitative accounts indicated that guided reflection encouraged participants to become active interpreters of their own sleep rather than passive recipients of information.
AI.conclusion: Guided reflection can make digital sleep technologies more personally meaningful and support users’ motivation to act. The paper also concludes that incorporating expert knowledge is an ongoing process: specialists must repeatedly externalize tacit judgments, operationalize them in the system, and make them testable, rather than simply transferring a fixed body of knowledge once.

title: Feeling Wistful: Reflecting on Scholarly Sensibilities with Creative Reading Traces
summary: Researchers often read before they can articulate what they are looking for. As AI increasingly mediates scholarly search and synthesis, understanding and preserving the idiosyncratic judgments guiding early exploration become important. We call these evolving orientations scholarly sensibilities. To understand curiosity-driven reading, we first examined Wikipedia rabbitholing, a self-directed browsing practice, then designed Wistful, a research probe for open-ended scholarly exploration that captures reading paths as creative reading traces. We studied Wistful with 16 HCI researchers---eight junior and eight senior---in comparison with their usual workflows. Researchers approached the same scholarly landscape differently, with familiarity and personal interests shaping what they pursued and semantic proximity and scholarly links shaping their paths. Their traces made these differences visible and let readers revisit and compare their paths. We position creative reading traces as artifacts for reflection and exchange and as a means of studying how scholarly sensibilities are expressed through reading.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how researchers’ personal interests and familiarity shape curiosity-driven scholarly exploration. It introduces Wistful, a research probe that records browsing trajectories as creative reading traces, showing that these traces can support reflection, comparison, and the study of scholarly sensibilities.
AI.motivation: AI-mediated scholarly search and synthesis may obscure the subjective, evolving judgments researchers use when exploring unfamiliar literature. The paper aims to understand and preserve these early exploratory orientations—termed scholarly sensibilities—by studying self-directed browsing and making reading paths inspectable.
AI.method: The researchers first examined Wikipedia rabbitholing as an example of self-directed exploratory browsing. They then designed Wistful, a probe for open-ended scholarly exploration that records users’ reading paths as creative reading traces. They conducted a comparative study with 16 HCI researchers, including eight junior and eight senior participants, contrasting Wistful with participants’ usual research workflows.
AI.result: Participants explored the same scholarly landscape in substantially different ways. Familiarity and personal interests influenced which materials they pursued, while semantic proximity and scholarly links shaped the progression of their paths. The recorded traces made these individual differences visible and enabled participants to revisit and compare their exploratory processes.
AI.conclusion: Creative reading traces can function as reflective and communicative artifacts, allowing researchers to inspect and exchange accounts of scholarly exploration. They also provide a means for studying how scholarly sensibilities are expressed through reading behavior, particularly during open-ended, curiosity-driven inquiry.

title: Intent Graph: Navigating the Analytical Reasoning Space for Exploratory Data Analysis
summary: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is rarely open-ended in practice: analysts work from high-level domain questions toward the concrete analyses that can answer them, prioritizing directions with domain knowledge and prior hypotheses. Large language models (LLMs) can supply such knowledge, but their responses are unstructured, leaving analysts no way to see what has been explored, what is missing, or why one direction was chosen over another. We present DAG-EDA, a system that lets analysts and an LLM co-navigate the space of possible analyses through two linked structures. An intent graph, governed by a grammar of analytical intent, decomposes an ambiguous natural-language question into progressively concrete analysis tasks, keeping alternative framings open and letting analysts branch, backtrack, and compare paths. A multi-layered knowledge graph externalizes the LLM's domain knowledge, linking domain concepts to the dataset variables that can measure them, so analysts can inspect and contest how their question is grounded in the data. Both graphs are constructed from only the dataset and the analyst's question, and the analyses the analyst reaches are rendered as interactive dashboards. We illustrate the system through a usage scenario and describe a user study design for examining whether the system scaffold analysts' reasoning and navigation.

AI.tldr: DAG-EDA is a human–LLM co-navigation system for making exploratory data analysis more systematic, inspectable, and traceable. It uses an intent graph to organize analytical directions and a knowledge graph to connect domain concepts with measurable dataset variables, with resulting analyses presented as interactive dashboards.
AI.motivation: Conventional EDA is guided by high-level domain questions, prior hypotheses, and analyst expertise rather than being fully open-ended. Although LLMs can contribute useful domain knowledge, their unstructured responses do not reveal which analytical possibilities have been explored, which remain unexplored, or why a particular direction was selected. DAG-EDA is motivated by the need to externalize analytical reasoning and LLM knowledge so analysts can navigate, compare, branch, backtrack, and challenge the grounding of analyses in the data.
AI.method: DAG-EDA builds two linked structures from the analyst’s natural-language question and the dataset. First, an intent graph uses a grammar of analytical intent to progressively decompose an ambiguous question into increasingly concrete analysis tasks while preserving alternative framings. Second, a multi-layered knowledge graph represents domain concepts and links them to dataset variables that can operationalize those concepts. Analysts co-navigate these structures with the LLM, and selected analyses are rendered as interactive dashboards. The paper illustrates the system through a usage scenario and proposes a user-study design to evaluate its effects on analysts’ reasoning and navigation.
AI.result: The abstract reports a system demonstration and a planned evaluation rather than completed empirical findings. It shows that DAG-EDA can represent alternative analytical paths, support branching and backtracking, expose how domain concepts are mapped to data variables, and produce interactive dashboard-based analyses. The user study is described as a design for future examination of whether these features scaffold analysts’ reasoning and navigation.
AI.conclusion: DAG-EDA offers a structured, transparent approach to human–LLM collaboration in EDA. By linking analytical intent with explicit domain-to-data grounding, it aims to make exploratory reasoning more visible, contestable, and navigable. However, the abstract does not yet establish effectiveness because the user study results are not reported.

title: Magic Pen: Automatic Pen Mode Switching for Document Annotation
summary: Traditional digital pen interfaces use menu buttons to change the pen mode, which results in time and cognitive load spent on round-trip interactions and mode errors from tapping small mode selection buttons. This work presents the Magic Pen, a technique which uses machine learning to automatically switch between digital pen modes without requiring explicit mode changes. Magic Pen is driven by an LSTM model trained on pen data collected from 27 participants across two studies and uses transfer learning to iteratively tune the model towards how a specific user annotates. Error mitigation techniques using a flick gesture or on-screen tap are incorporated to correct mode errors or remove a stroke quickly. We evaluated Magic Pen in a comparative study with 18 participants, followed by iterative improvements and a deployment study with 8 participants. Magic Pen was preferred compared to a conventional menu-based approach, and transfer learning allowed for greater model predictability and stability.

AI.tldr: Magic Pen is a machine-learning-based digital pen interface that automatically switches pen modes from user strokes, reducing explicit menu interaction and mode-selection errors. An LSTM model trained on data from 27 participants is adapted to individual users through transfer learning. Studies indicate that users preferred Magic Pen over a conventional menu-based interface, while adaptation improved prediction stability and reliability.
AI.motivation: Conventional digital pen interfaces require users to select modes through small menu buttons. These explicit round-trip interactions increase task time and cognitive load, and they can cause mode errors when users tap the wrong control or fail to change modes correctly. The paper is motivated by the need for a more fluid and less interruption-prone pen interaction technique.
AI.method: The authors propose Magic Pen, which automatically infers and switches pen modes using an LSTM model trained on pen-input data collected from 27 participants in two studies. Transfer learning incrementally adapts the model to an individual user’s annotation behavior. The system also includes error-mitigation mechanisms: a flick gesture for correcting mode errors and an on-screen tap for rapidly removing a stroke. Evaluation consisted of a comparative study with 18 participants, followed by iterative refinement and a deployment study with 8 participants.
AI.result: Participants preferred Magic Pen to the conventional menu-based approach. Transfer learning improved model predictability and stability for individual users. The abstract does not provide quantitative performance measures, such as accuracy, task time, error rate, or statistical significance.
AI.conclusion: Automatic mode switching can make digital pen interaction more seamless and preferable than explicit menu-based mode selection. User-specific adaptation through transfer learning appears important for maintaining reliable predictions, while dedicated correction mechanisms help address inevitable classification errors.

title: SpheriColor: Colormaps for Spherical Geospatial Input Topographies
comment: 4 Pages, 3 Figures, to be published in IEEE Visualization Conference (VIS)
summary: Multivariate geospatial data visualization often relies on multiple coordinated views, where color can be used to either link views or encode data attributes. Encoding spatial locations through color can reveal patterns in non-spatial visualizations, yet most applications of colormaps focus on high-dimensional attribute encodings instead. While 2D colormaps have been studied extensively, color encodings designed for spherical geospatial data have received much less attention, even though all locations lie on a sphere. To address this, we propose SpheriColor, a colormap generation approach for mapping geospatial references guided by the design goals of distance preservation and colorspace exploitation. We project a geospatial distance function into a perceptually linear colorspace, followed by two different gamut-constrained optimization strategies. We perform a quantitative evaluation using both real-world and synthetic datasets, demonstrating superior performance over 2D colormaps and HSLuv double cone encodings. The simplex-based optimization excels at distance preservation, whereas the ray-based approach provides better colorspace exploitation.

AI.tldr: SpheriColor is a colormap-generation method for encoding spherical geospatial locations in color. It projects geospatial distances into a perceptually linear color space and uses gamut-constrained optimization to balance distance preservation and color-space utilization. Evaluation on real and synthetic data shows it outperforms 2D colormaps and HSLuv double-cone encodings; simplex optimization favors distance fidelity, while ray optimization favors gamut exploitation.
AI.motivation: Existing multivariate geospatial visualization systems often use color to encode attributes or coordinate views, but location-based color encodings are less developed. Most established colormaps are designed for planar 2D domains and do not adequately account for the spherical geometry of the Earth. The paper therefore seeks a method that preserves geospatial relationships perceptually while making effective use of the available color gamut.
AI.method: SpheriColor maps locations on a sphere by projecting a geospatial distance function into a perceptually linear color space. Because not all projected colors are displayable, it applies two gamut-constrained optimization strategies: a simplex-based approach and a ray-based approach. The two strategies represent different trade-offs between preserving pairwise distances and exploiting the available color space.
AI.result: Quantitative experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets show that SpheriColor performs better than conventional 2D colormaps and HSLuv double-cone encodings. The simplex-based optimization achieves stronger distance preservation, whereas the ray-based optimization makes better use of the color space.
AI.conclusion: Color encodings for spherical geospatial references can be improved by explicitly modeling spherical distance and perceptual color-space constraints. SpheriColor provides two complementary optimization variants: simplex optimization is preferable when geographic distance fidelity is the priority, while ray optimization is preferable when maximizing color-space utilization is more important.

title: Design Creativity Bench: Measuring creativity in LLM-Generated UI
summary: As leading LLMs improve on capability evaluations, their limitations in producing creative outputs on design tasks remain insufficiently characterised. Our work introduces Design Creativity Bench, a benchmark that evaluates diversity and appropriateness in UI designs. It measures distinctiveness among models on the same prompt (originality), how much a model's designs change between two prompts for the same UI goal in different product domains (creative range), and the share of a brief's acceptance criteria each design meets (appropriateness). Originality is 0.592 for same-prompt design pairs from different models (95% CI [0.582, 0.602]), far below the 0.764 for same-prompt human-model pairs (95% CI [0.751, 0.778]). Creative range is 0.581 across models (95% CI [0.567, 0.597]), against 0.902 for human designs (95% CI [0.884, 0.919]). Appropriateness is above 90% for every model, and the best model reaches 99.2%, slightly above the 98.0% for human designs. Our work shows that the default output of LLMs, though generally appropriate, is substantially more repetitive than the human baseline. This calls for strong measures to address the issue.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Design Creativity Bench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated UI design creativity along three dimensions: originality, creative range, and appropriateness. Results show that LLM outputs are generally highly appropriate but substantially less diverse and flexible than human designs.
AI.motivation: Although leading LLMs perform well on capability benchmarks, their ability to generate creative designs is not well characterized. Existing evaluations tend to emphasize correctness or task completion rather than whether outputs are distinctive, adaptable across contexts, and suitable for a design brief. The paper addresses this gap by establishing a systematic benchmark for UI design creativity.
AI.method: The authors create Design Creativity Bench and evaluate UI designs using three metrics: (1) originality, measuring distinctiveness between designs generated by different models from the same prompt; (2) creative range, measuring how much a model changes its designs when the same UI goal is placed in different product domains; and (3) appropriateness, measuring the proportion of a brief's acceptance criteria satisfied by each design. Model results are compared with human-generated designs, with 95% confidence intervals reported for the diversity metrics.
AI.result: LLM-generated designs show lower diversity than human designs. Originality is 0.592 for same-prompt designs from different models, compared with 0.764 for human-model pairs. Creative range is 0.581 across models, compared with 0.902 for human designs. In contrast, appropriateness exceeds 90% for all models; the best model achieves 99.2%, slightly higher than the human score of 98.0%.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are effective at satisfying explicit UI design requirements but tend to produce repetitive outputs and adapt less creatively across domains than humans. The findings indicate that standard LLM generation produces a creativity deficit primarily in diversity and contextual variation, motivating methods that explicitly promote originality and broader creative exploration.

title: NeuroDivSim: An Interactive Tool for Model-Based Reflection on Cognitive Diversity in Interface Design
summary: Recent approaches to simulated and synthetic users offer new ways to support design, but raise questions about how computational representations of users should contribute to design practice. We present NeuroDivSim, an interactive tool that explores simulation as an inspectable mechanism for reflecting on cognitive diversity during design and prototyping. Rather than using an LLM to act as a simulated user, NeuroDivSim uses generative AI to construct inspectable task, interface, and environment models from a usage scenario. After human review, these models are combined with explicit cognitive reference configurations and processed through deterministic simulation. This enables designers to hold a modeled usage situation constant while varying cognitive assumptions and tracing their consequences to interaction steps and rule-based design recommendations. We further report an exploratory pilot evaluation (N=10) that provided formative insights into how participants engaged with the workflow and informed subsequent refinements to the presentation of models, simulation results, and recommendations.

AI.tldr: NeuroDivSim is an interactive design-support tool that uses generative AI to build inspectable models of a usage scenario and deterministic simulation to examine how explicit cognitive configurations affect interaction outcomes and design recommendations. A small exploratory pilot (N=10) produced formative feedback for refining the workflow and result presentation.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the need for more transparent and practically useful ways to incorporate simulated or synthetic users into design. It focuses on cognitive diversity and the concern that computational user representations should be inspectable, rather than functioning as opaque agents whose behavior is difficult to interpret or connect to design decisions.
AI.method: NeuroDivSim uses generative AI to construct inspectable task, interface, and environment models from a usage scenario. Human reviewers validate or refine these models, which are then combined with explicit cognitive reference configurations and processed using deterministic simulation. Designers can keep the modeled usage situation fixed, vary cognitive assumptions, trace effects through interaction steps, and receive rule-based design recommendations. An exploratory pilot with 10 participants evaluated engagement with the workflow and informed refinements to model, simulation-result, and recommendation presentation.
AI.result: The pilot generated formative insights into how participants used and understood the workflow. These insights led to subsequent refinements in the presentation of models, simulation outputs, and recommendations. The abstract does not report quantitative performance results, statistical tests, or evidence of improved design quality.
AI.conclusion: NeuroDivSim demonstrates a transparent alternative to LLM-based simulated users by separating generative model construction from deterministic, inspectable simulation. Its main contribution is a framework for systematically examining the design consequences of different cognitive assumptions, although the early pilot indicates that further validation is needed.

title: STcubeOperator: A Framework for Analyzing Spatiotemporal Event Data
summary: The analysis of spatiotemporal event data is essential for informed decision-making in domains such as disaster response, conflict analysis, or intelligence investigations. However, the complexity and interdependence of spatial, temporal, and multiple thematic attributes pose significant challenges for both analysis and visualization. While space-time cubes (STCs) present a powerful integrated visualization technique to analyze this kind of data, existing approaches often lack support for complex exploratory workflows, thus limiting the ability to derive meaningful insights. We address this gap by introducing STcubeOperator, a novel framework that models analysis tasks through space-time cube operations, considering them in context of visualizations, interactions, and computational choices, and implement them in an interactive visual analytics environment. By expressing analysis tasks as a sequence of multiple elementary operations--such as filtering, chopping, and flattening--our approach enables analysts to dynamically explore data from different perspectives. We further provide an open-source prototype implementing the operations in a 3D interactive environment to facilitate task-based exploratory analysis of spatiotemporal event data. We demonstrate the applicability of our framework with a case study based on real-world data on strategic and military operations in the Russia-Ukrainian War, showing its capabilities to reveal spatiotemporal patterns. An expert user study (n=8) shows how specific tasks can be solved with our framework, highlights the versatility of our approach, and provides valuable insights on which operations experienced analysts utilize in practice.

AI.tldr: This paper presents STcubeOperator, a framework for exploratory analysis of spatiotemporal event data using composable space-time cube operations in an interactive visual analytics environment.
AI.motivation: Existing space-time cube approaches do not adequately support complex, iterative exploratory workflows involving spatial, temporal, and thematic attributes. The paper aims to make such analyses more systematic, flexible, and task-oriented.
AI.method: The authors model analytical tasks as sequences of elementary space-time cube operations, including filtering, chopping, and flattening. These operations are linked to visualizations, user interactions, and computational choices, and are implemented in an open-source 3D interactive prototype. The framework is evaluated through a real-world case study and an expert user study with eight participants.
AI.result: The prototype supports dynamic exploration from multiple perspectives and demonstrates the ability to reveal spatiotemporal patterns. The expert study shows that the framework can support specific analytical tasks, is versatile, and captures the operations used by experienced analysts.
AI.conclusion: STcubeOperator provides a task-based framework for interactive exploratory analysis of spatiotemporal event data. Its composable operations and integrated visual environment address limitations of existing space-time cube tools, while the user study offers practical evidence about analyst workflows and operation usage.

title: "Hot-Blooded" vs "Cold-Blooded": Simulating the Behavioral Phenotypes of Childhood Aggression via Generative Agents
summary: This study examines the construct validity of LLM-based generative agents in simulating reactive, proactive, and co-occurring aggression in children. Four distinct agents were instantiated using a theory-driven parameterization grounded in the social information processing model. A total of 1,920 simulation runs were conducted across eight social scenarios, employing a hybrid blind-coding pipeline to extract 32 quantitative behavioral indicators. Results demonstrate robust discriminant validity relative to a non-aggressive baseline, with large effect sizes. High cross-seed reliability confirms that behavioral differentiation is driven by underlying psychological parameters rather than model stochasticity. Qualitative narrative analyses further converged with established empirical literature. Overall, these findings indicate that theory-parameterized LLM agents can accurately reproduce distinct aggression subtypes, offering a scalable, highly controllable framework for hypothesis generation, intervention piloting, and the refinement of psychological measurement tools.

AI.tldr: The study evaluates whether theory-parameterized LLM agents can validly simulate distinct forms of child aggression. Across 1,920 runs and eight scenarios, the agents showed strong behavioral separation from a non-aggressive baseline, high cross-seed reliability, and qualitative alignment with prior psychological research. The framework appears promising for controlled hypothesis generation and intervention prototyping, although the abstract does not establish real-world predictive validity.
AI.motivation: The study is motivated by the need for scalable and controllable computational models of child aggression that distinguish reactive, proactive, and co-occurring forms. It addresses whether LLM-based generative agents can represent theoretically meaningful psychological differences rather than merely producing stochastic or superficially plausible behavior.
AI.method: Four LLM agents were instantiated using theory-driven parameters derived from the social information processing model. They were evaluated over 1,920 simulation runs spanning eight social scenarios. A hybrid blind-coding pipeline extracted 32 quantitative behavioral indicators, which were used to assess discriminant validity and cross-seed reliability against a non-aggressive baseline. Qualitative narrative analyses were also compared with established empirical literature.
AI.result: The agents demonstrated robust discriminant validity relative to the non-aggressive baseline, with large effect sizes. High cross-seed reliability suggested that behavioral differences were attributable to the underlying psychological parameterization rather than random model variation. Qualitative outputs also converged with prior empirical findings.
AI.conclusion: Theory-parameterized LLM agents may provide a scalable, controllable framework for modeling aggression subtypes and supporting hypothesis generation, intervention piloting, and psychological measurement development. However, the abstract supports construct validity within simulation more directly than ecological or predictive validity in real children.

title: Hybrid Cinematography: Previsualizing and Managing Hallucination Risk in Generative Video Reshooting
summary: On a film set, the camera move is committed during a take. Generative video reshooting lets filmmakers change it afterward, but may require hallucinating unrecorded content, a gap sometimes discovered only after leaving the set. We present Hybrid Cinematography, a workflow that bridges physical capture and generative reshooting to manage hallucination risk while filmmakers can still act on it. Using an editable 3D shot plan and a proxy of the take, our previsualization evaluates hallucination risk in real time. Seeing where the take lacks support, filmmakers can iteratively adjust the plan, explore moves that balance capture and generation, shoot guided pickups, or knowingly accept hallucination. We demonstrate the workflow through a mobile augmented reality application for on-set planning, capture, and review, and an offline pipeline for existing video. A study with experienced filmmakers reveals how previsualizing risk informs camera decisions and exposes tensions between creative intent and generative hallucination.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Hybrid Cinematography, a workflow that helps filmmakers assess and manage the risk of hallucinated content when modifying camera movements with generative video tools after filming.
AI.motivation: Generative video reshooting can alter a committed camera move, but it may need to invent visual content that was not captured. Filmmakers may discover this lack of supporting footage too late, so the paper aims to provide early, actionable feedback about hallucination risk during production.
AI.method: The workflow combines physical capture with generative reshooting through an editable 3D shot plan and a proxy of the filmed take. It provides real-time previsualization of where the recorded footage lacks support, enabling filmmakers to revise the shot plan, explore camera moves that balance capture and generation, record guided pickup shots, or intentionally accept hallucination. The authors implement the workflow in a mobile augmented-reality application for on-set planning, capture, and review, along with an offline pipeline for existing videos, and evaluate it with experienced filmmakers.
AI.result: The study shows that visualizing hallucination risk influences filmmakers’ camera decisions and helps reveal unsupported regions of a shot before or during production. It also exposes tensions between filmmakers’ creative intentions and the limitations or uncertainty introduced by generative video.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid Cinematography provides a practical bridge between conventional filming and generative reshooting by making hallucination risk visible and actionable. Rather than eliminating generation-related uncertainty, it supports informed trade-offs among capture, reshooting, creative intent, and intentional use of hallucinated content.
